client: I've been having a really hard time since my brother died six months ago. Every time I go out with friends or someone invites me somewhere, I just feel this hollow emptiness, like I'm going through the motions but not actually present. I guess I'm here because people keep telling me therapy helps, but honestly I'm not sure anything can really touch what I'm feeling right now.
therapist: What you're carrying sounds incredibly heavy — the loss of your brother, and then this painful disconnect of being surrounded by people yet feeling utterly absent from it all. Your voice carries that exhaustion too, like you're holding something vast and quiet inside, even as the words come quickly, as if you've been waiting to let some of this out. It makes complete sense that you'd feel skeptical about whether anything can reach a grief this deep, and I want you to know that doubt is welcome here — we don't have to fix anything today, just start by making space for what's real for you.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Yeah, I... I didn't expect to feel anything saying it out loud, but there's this tightness in my chest right now that kind of surprised me. Like I've been carrying this story around for so long that it almost felt like it belonged to someone else, but hearing you reflect it back makes it suddenly very real and very mine again. I'm not sure if that's a good thing or if I just want to go home and not feel any of this.
therapist: That tightness in your chest is actually something really significant — it's your grief recognizing itself, saying *"this is mine, this is real,"* and that takes courage to sit with even for a moment. The part of you that wants to go home and shut it all out makes complete sense too; you've been protecting yourself with that distance, and it's kept you functioning for six months. What if both things could be true at once — that feeling it is painful *and* that letting it be yours again is the first honest step toward not being so alone with it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that, but I'm not sure sitting with it is actually going to help. Like, what if I let myself really feel it and then I just... can't stop? I've kept this grief at arm's length for six months because every time it gets close, it feels like it could swallow me whole.
therapist: The fear in your voice right now — that quickened pace, the tension underneath your words — tells me this isn't just a thought for you, it's something that feels genuinely dangerous, like standing at the edge of something with no bottom. That fear of being swallowed is one of the most common and most human responses to profound grief, and it makes complete sense that you've built walls to keep it manageable. But here's what CBT and neuroscience both show us: feelings, even the most overwhelming ones, are actually waves — they peak and they pass — and part of what we'd do together is practice feeling just a little at a time, so you build evidence that you *can* hold this without it consuming you.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying about feelings being like waves, and part of me wants to believe that, I really do. But honestly, when I think about actually letting myself go there — letting myself really feel how alone I've been since my dad died — it doesn't feel like a wave, it feels like I'd just... disappear into it. And I guess I'm skeptical that doing it "a little at a time" would actually work for me, because what if I start and I can't stop?
therapist: I notice you said your dad just now — and I want to gently hold that with you, because it sounds like this grief may be even larger than we first named together. Your voice is soft but moving quickly, like part of you is bracing even as you speak, and that image of disappearing rather than just feeling — that tells me how alone and unwitnessed this pain has been. What if the goal isn't to "go there" all at once, but simply to notice that right now, in this moment, you said something true and real — and you're still here.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I didn't expect to feel anything when you said that, but something kind of... shifted, I guess. Like, I've been talking around my dad for weeks and you just said it plainly, and now my chest feels tight in a way that's uncomfortable but also maybe not entirely bad. I'm still not sure what "still being here" is supposed to mean for me, though — it sounds reassuring but I don't quite feel it yet.
therapist: That shift you're describing — uncomfortable but not entirely bad — is actually really important, and I want to stay right there with you for a moment, because that's not nothing. Your voice has a kind of quiet openness to it right now, like something has loosened just slightly, even as you're still figuring out what it means. "Still being here" doesn't have to feel reassuring yet — it just means that the tightness came, and you stayed, and we're still talking, and that's the first small piece of evidence that you can hold more than you thought.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that "still being here" means something. But honestly, my first instinct is to push back a little — like, staying doesn't feel like an accomplishment, it just feels like... what else would I do? I guess I'm not sure I trust myself to actually hold onto this feeling once I walk out of here and I'm alone again with all the same thoughts.
therapist: That soft, almost tentative way you're speaking right now — like you're testing whether it's safe to say this out loud — tells me this fear of losing the feeling once you're alone is very real and very present for you. And I want to gently challenge one thing: you called staying "what else would I do," but that's actually your mind minimizing something — you've had six months of reasons to shut down and disappear, and instead you're here, pushing back, staying honest, which is its own quiet form of strength. What if we spent a little time before you leave today thinking about one small, concrete thing you could return to when you're alone — not to fix the grief, but just to remind yourself that this moment happened and was real?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I appreciate you saying that, I really do, but part of me wants to push back on the "strength" thing because it doesn't feel like strength from the inside, it just feels like... not knowing what else to do. And the idea of finding something concrete to hold onto when I'm alone sounds nice in theory, but every time I've tried things like that before, like journaling or whatever, it just ends up feeling hollow and kind of pathetic, like I'm performing comfort for myself. I guess I'm worried that whatever we come up with here will feel meaningful in this room and then completely fall apart the second I close my front door behind me.
therapist: The speed and intensity in your voice right now — like the words are almost outrunning something — tells me this fear of things falling apart the moment you're alone isn't abstract, it feels urgent and very familiar. And I want to sit with what you said about journaling feeling like "performing comfort for yourself," because that's actually a really sharp observation — it tells me you need something that feels *true*, not soothing, and that's a different and more honest starting point than most people bring. What if the thing you take home isn't a practice or a technique, but just this: that today you said your dad's name out loud, your chest got tight, and you didn't disappear — and that's not a performance, that actually happened?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: That's... I don't know, when you put it that way it doesn't feel as small as I've been making it. But I'm also sitting here thinking, okay, I said his name, my chest got tight, and then what — I go home to my apartment and it's just quiet again, and that quiet has a way of undoing things really fast. I guess I'm scared that whatever just happened in here won't travel with me past the parking lot.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — fast, pitched high, like you're trying to stay ahead of something — tells me that quiet apartment isn't just a place, it's where the grief has the most power over you, and that's a really important thing to name. And I hear the fear that this moment won't travel, but I want to offer something small and true: the quiet doesn't undo what happened here, it just makes it harder to hear — and what you said his name, and your chest tightened, and you stayed, that's already in you now, not in this room. So maybe the question isn't how to hold onto this feeling, but how to be just a little less alone with the quiet — and that's something we can actually work on together.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it — that I already carry something from this. But when I'm back in that apartment and it's 11pm and there's no one to text, I don't know if "being less alone with the quiet" is something I can actually do, like what does that even look like in practice? It sounds meaningful here, but I'm scared it's just going to feel like another thing I'm failing at when I'm by myself.
therapist: That very high pitch in your voice right now, even as your pace steadies, tells me this isn't hypothetical for you — 11pm in that apartment is a real and specific kind of lonely you've already lived many times. And I want to gently name something: you just framed "being less alone with the quiet" as another thing you might *fail at*, and that instinct to turn even small steps into tests you can lose tells me how exhausted your inner critic has made you. So what if instead of a practice, we just named one true thing you could say to yourself at 11pm — not to feel better, but just to be honest, something like *"this is hard, and I said his name today, and that was real"* — no performance, no passing or failing, just one true sentence?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me actually wants to hold onto that idea, but another part immediately goes "okay but what if even that feels hollow when I'm actually sitting there at 11pm." Like, I'm already imagining saying it and it just echoing off the walls and feeling stupid. I think that's what scares me most, that even the honest things stop feeling real when there's no one there to receive them.
therapist: The urgency in your voice right now — fast, loud, almost like you're racing to name the fear before it catches you — tells me you just touched something really core: that grief without a witness can make even true things feel like they're disappearing into the air. And what you just described, honest words echoing off walls with no one to receive them, that's not a failure of the technique, that's actually the heart of what you're grieving — not just your dad, but the specific person who may have been someone who received you. That's worth bringing back here next time, because that's not a problem to solve with a sentence at 11pm — that's something we can actually grieve together, slowly, in a place where your words don't have to echo.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very loud, very rapid speech
